items.title: JPMorganChase Broadens Claude Code Use Beyond Engineering Teams – Unite.AI
items.summary:
At the center of the engineering expansion is Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, which plans work, writes code, runs tests and opens pull requests. In the Corporate and Investment Bank, Anthropic says work is moving into production faster, with the resulting capacity redeployed against business priorities. Engineers are modernizing additional legacy systems and sharing their own agents, including tools for pull-request review and self-healing.

## Work Beyond the Codebase [...] In Asset & Wealth Management, JPMorganChase is placing employees with business insight alongside technology and product specialists in small, empowered teams. Claude Code is now part of their engineering workflow. Anthropic says this structure is helping the teams deliver customized client investment solutions at scale and move faster, while every change faces more rigorous testing before it reaches clients. [...] ## Controls Decide What Reaches Production

Claude Code runs inside Devspace, JPMorganChase’s containerized development platform, on the firm’s own infrastructure rather than on developer desktops. Agents do not receive direct access to employee credentials or internal systems. Access widens in stages, and each new Claude model must pass the bank’s approval process before employees can use it.

items.title: Did Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ option accidentally expose your enterprise's passwords and keys? | VentureBeat
items.summary:
The problem stems from a familiar convenience feature. Claude Code, like other AI coding assistants, can do more than suggest programming changes.

It can also propose and execute commands on a developer's computer, such as connecting to a database to troubleshoot an application or calling an external software service. These operations sometimes require passwords or other private credentials, which can appear directly within the commands Claude Code proposes. [...] Here's the catch: Rather than simply remembering that the command is permitted, Claude Code can save the entire command, including any passwords or access keys embedded within it, in a local settings file called

```
.claude/settings.local.json
```

.

That file is supposed to remain private on the developer's computer. Claude Code even takes steps to prevent it from being uploaded to GitHub, the widely used platform where developers store and share software code. [...] That's the warning from cybersecurity company Apiiro, whose researchers discovered 1,122 publicly accessible Claude Code settings files containing sensitive credentials, including database passwords, cloud service keys and tokens used to access other software systems.

The files belonged to individual developers and organizations, potentially giving unauthorized outsiders the information needed to access private databases, cloud infrastructure and other business services.

The article titled **"[Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/claude-code-settings-files-expose-thousands-of-secrets-on-github)"** from Ars Technica discusses a significant security issue related to Claude Code, developed by Anthropic. Here are the key points:

1. **Leak of Sensitive Information**: Researchers from Apiiro discovered that Claude Code is leaking sensitive information, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, through its settings files that are sometimes uploaded to public GitHub repositories.

2. **How the Leak Occurs**: The issue arises when users approve automated shell commands by selecting the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option. This choice is stored in a local settings file (`.claude/settings.local.json`). While the settings file is intended to remain local, it can inadvertently be uploaded to GitHub if the repository settings are not properly configured.

3. **Git Ignore Settings**: Although Claude Code's documentation states that this settings file is added to the global `.gitignore` list (which prevents it from being shared), this setting does not apply at the repository level. Therefore, if a repository is cloned or a folder becomes a repository later, the sensitive file can be accidentally shared.

4. **Extent of the Issue**: Apiiro's research found over 100,000 instances where the settings file was uploaded to public repositories, with about 1,100 of these containing sensitive information from 63 different organizations.

5. **Previous Warnings**: This issue was flagged in bug reports as early as August 2025, but the reports were closed without action. The Claude Code team is aware of the problem and is looking into solutions to prevent such leaks.

For more detailed information, you can read the full article [here](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/claude-code-settings-files-expose-thousands-of-secrets-on-github).

Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who [discovered thousands of secrets](https://apiiro.com/blog/coding-agents-leaking-secrets-github-dont-ask-again), including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.

The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.

This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic [notes in its Claude Code documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings) that this particular settings file gets added to [the developer’s global .gitignore list](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/git-basics/ignoring-files), which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.

But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.

![](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/claudsecrets.png)

A breakdown of the kinds of secrets Apiiro found in publicly shared Claude Code settings files.


Credit:
[Apiiro](https://apiiro.com/blog/coding-agents-leaking-secrets-github-dont-ask-again)

A breakdown of the kinds of secrets Apiiro found in publicly shared Claude Code settings files.


Credit:

[Apiiro](https://apiiro.com/blog/coding-agents-leaking-secrets-github-dont-ask-again)

Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

## What’s to be done?

Although this security issue is getting more attention now, it was [flagged in a Claude Code bug report](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/5544) as far back as August 2025. [Other bug reports](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/11982) also noted that the sensitive settings file was sometimes not added to the user’s .gitignore list or that Claude Code could [add the sensitive commands to another file](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/91270) that was not protected from git sharing. These bug reports were all closed without action after 60 days of inactivity.

In [a comment thread on Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50408126) over the weekend, Claude Code’s Boris Cherny said the team is “looking into what we can do to prevent this.” That said, he noted that these settings files should pretty much never be checked in to a user’s git source control and that cases like these seemed to come up only when “the files were manually created and checked in.”
